description: A self-contained OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect provider for ASP.NET Core. Two lines in Program.cs give you authorization code + PKCE, refresh tokens, client credentials, the device grant, PAR, introspection, revocation, dynamic client registration, RP-initiated logout and a discovery document any standard OIDC library can configure itself from. Multi-tenant, runs on SQLite, MySQL or PostgreSQL, and ships its own sign-in, consent and admin UI. Pair it with Ark.oAuth.Client for the application side.
releaseNotes:
2.4.5 — the identity server is an MCP server. On by default; nothing answers without a credential.

Apart from the security changes, sign-in, discovery, tokens, pages, the management API and existing
configuration are as in 2.4.2.
* **Security: upgrade promptly.** A confidential client whose secret was never set, above all the seeded
  {tenant}_machine client, could be authenticated as; every release since 2.0 is affected. It is now always
  refused. On a server not yet upgraded, press Regenerate secret on each such client. The private signing
  key is no longer returned inside client and mapping rows. The lockout holds for parallel attempts. A
  password change ends that account's sessions and refresh tokens. The setup code is asked for outside
  Development on localhost too, and a configured server never falls back into setup. The v1 token endpoint
  refuses a client that has a credential (Oidc:AllowConfidentialClientsAtV1Token while one is still on v1).
  An account another tenant manages cannot be made an administrator over MCP. All of it, with what to check
  before and after upgrading, is under "Next release" in MIGRATION.md.
* **Set the server up with an agent.** While it is unconfigured, /ark-idp/mcp offers the setup wizard
  as tools, with the setup code as the bearer token. Values are collected section by section, in any
  order and over several conversations, each with who supplied it; tested; reviewed; and installed
  only as reviewed. The administrator sets their own password through a one-time link.
* **A setup link, for whoever cannot read the server log.** With ark_oauth_server:Setup:AccessKey set
  (16 characters or more), {address}/ark-idp/setup#key={AccessKey} opens the wizard with the setup code
  filled in, through POST /ark-idp/setup/api/code. The setup code is then derived from the key: the same
  on every instance and after every restart. Wrong keys are answered one a second, past 20 waiting with
  429, and each code handed out is logged. Once setup is finished the link answers 404 like the rest of
  the wizard. Without the setting nothing changes.
* **Three levels after that**, each its own endpoint: /ark-idp/mcp for the operator, /{tenant}/mcp
  for a tenant's administrator (applications, people, access, agents, sessions, keys, audit), and
  /{tenant}/mcp/{client_id} for one application, its people and the agents it lists. The machine
  credential opens the first two. Server card, client configuration and protected resource metadata
  (RFC 9728) are served beside each.
* **Resource indicators (RFC 8707) for these endpoints**, on every grant: the token's aud is the
  endpoint, and nothing else accepts it. Every other value of resource is handled as before.
* **Two scopes, mcp.read and mcp.manage**, step up with HTTP 403. mcp.manage cannot be
  self-registered. Administrators over MCP hold ark.host.admin, ark.tenant.admin or
  ark.client.admin on an access mapping.
* **Tenants get administrators of their own.** tenant_create returns a machine credential that
  reaches that tenant and nothing else. users.home_tenant_id says which tenant manages an account;
  null, which is every existing one, is the operator.
* **Every change over MCP, and every call refused for want of permission, is recorded**, whatever
  EnableLogTrace says.
* **The onboarding agent is included.** The setup wizard's first page links to Ark Pilot (/ark-agent),
  which collects the same answers in a chat, hands sections to colleagues by link, and shows what is
  waiting for a person. It runs only while the server is unconfigured; a configured server has no route,
  client or thread of it. No model is used unless ark_onboarding_agent:Llm names one. The package
  carries a second assembly, Ark.Agents.TenantOnboarding. ark_onboarding_agent:Enabled=false removes it.
* **The console lists every MCP endpoint**, for the operator, at /{tenant}/admin/mcp: search, filter by
  tenant and level, and open the documents of each in a new tab. GET /api/oauth/v1/mcp/endpoints
  returns the same list.
* Settings under ark_oauth_server:Mcp (Enabled, HostLevel, TenantLevel, ClientLevel, ReadOnly,
  AllowClientSecret, MaxRequestKilobytes). See MCP.md.
* Discovery is also served at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/{tenant} and
  /.well-known/openid-configuration/{tenant} (RFC 8414, issuer with a path).
* **Schema:** four nullable columns and two catalogue scopes, added on the first start.
* **Fixed:** on a new database, a host with AddArkWebhooks() whose first request came some seconds
  after start-up never got its schema, and every request failed. No new dependency.

2.4.2 — agent-to-agent (A2A) tokens. Inert until an operator lists a caller.

Every existing endpoint, token and page is as in 2.4.1, and a client that never asks for an agent
token sees no difference.
* **A token addressed to one agent.** `client_credentials` with `audience` (or `resource`) naming a
  client issues an access token whose `aud` is that client_id, with the `ark_claims` the target
  granted the caller. Short-lived (Oidc:A2ATokenLifetimeSeconds, 300), never refreshed.
* **On behalf of a user: token exchange (RFC 8693).** An agent presents a user's access token it was
  issued, or an agent token addressed to it, and names the next agent. `sub` stays the user,
  `ark_claims` are the user's own at the target, `act` records every agent on the way, and the new
  token never outlives the one exchanged. Refused when the user has no access to the target, the
  account is deactivated, the session has ended, or the chain exceeds Oidc:A2AMaxDelegationDepth (4).
* **The target decides who may call it.** ArkClient.a2a_callers lists the calling clients, the
  claims each holds there and whether it may act for users; the client drawer of the console edits
  it. Empty on every existing client, so nothing is issued until someone lists a caller.
* **Agent Card.** GET {issuer}/a2a/agent-card-security serves the security section of an A2A Agent
  Card (A2A 1.0; ?spec=0.3 for the older shape).
* **Introspection** answers for an agent token to the agent it is addressed to and the client that
  obtained it, with `act` and `ark_claims`.
* **Schema:** one nullable column, clients.a2a_callers_, added on first start by the schema sync.
* **Behaviour change:** `audience` / `resource` on a client_credentials request used to be ignored;
  a value other than the tenant's own audience is now answered invalid_target unless it names an
  agent the caller may call. Oidc:EnableA2A = false restores the previous behaviour. See A2A.md.
* **Agents are marked.** "This client is an agent" in the client drawer (is_agent on the client
  record) shows an agent badge in the client list, with how many clients it may call and be called
  by, and an "agents only" filter. A label: the caller list still decides who may call whom.
  One more nullable column, clients.is_agent.
* **An audit trail outside the server, optional.** With ark_oauth_server:Watch:Endpoint and ApiKey
  set (the setup wizard has an "Audit trail" step that tests them), every audit line is sent,
  structured, to an ARK-RAPID Watch node through the Ark.Watch.Client package: sign-ins and
  refusals, tokens, revocations, sign-outs and every change made in the console or the management
  API. Agent-to-agent activity is recorded in full: each token issued or refused, who it was for,
  the whole act chain, the token it was exchanged from, each introspection, and each change to who
  may call an agent. Sending never blocks or fails a request; while the node is away events wait
  on disk. Without the two settings nothing is constructed and nothing changes. New dependency:
  Ark.Watch.Client 0.1.3. See the README, "Audit trail", and A2A.md, "The audit trail".
* **A refused agent-token request is now traced.** It used to leave no row in audit_trace.

2.4.1 — webhooks, opt-in. Nothing changes for a host that does not ask for them.

Endpoints, discovery, tokens, pages and existing configuration are as in 2.4.0, so every client that
works with a 2.4.0 provider works with 2.4.1, and the four client packages are unchanged.
* **`builder.Services.AddArkWebhooks()`** adds a Webhooks page to the admin console (operator only)
  and an API under /api/oauth/v1/webhooks. Without the call nothing of it runs: no tables, no
  background work, no console link, and its routes answer 404.
* **Events** for sign-ins (succeeded, failed, locked out, refused, signed out), token issuance and
  revocation, device approval, and user, client and tenant changes, plus your own through
  IArkWebhookPublisher. Raising one never blocks a request and never fails it.
* **Delivery** is database-backed: stored, signed per Standard Webhooks, retried with exponential,
  linear or fixed back-off, moved to a dead-letter queue when it cannot be delivered, and replayable
  by hand. An endpoint that fails a configured number of times in a row is disabled for its tenant
  and what was waiting is dead-lettered.
* **Authentication** to the receiver: Basic, a static token, a JWT minted per request (HS256, or
  RS256 with the tenant's signing key), or an OAuth 2.0 access token from a refresh token or client
  credentials, refreshed once across all instances. Custom headers. Secrets encrypted at rest.
* **Shard plan per endpoint**: shared, dedicated, hashed over 2-32 table sets and one or more
  databases, or monthly tables. Tables live beside, never inside, the IdP's schema.
* **Dispatcher**: a BackgroundService on every instance, compare-and-swap claims with leases,
  bounded concurrency per instance and per endpoint, retention housekeeping. See WEBHOOKS.md.
* Event hooks were added beside existing audit calls in the sign-in, token, revocation, logout,
  registration, device, management and provisioning endpoints; each is one call that does nothing
  unless the module is registered.

2.4.0 — built to hold 30,000 signed-in users, and to run on more than one instance.

Measured, not estimated: with 30,000 accounts in PostgreSQL the same test went from 78 to 159
sign-ins a second and from 352 to 2,308 requests a second on one instance, and two instances behind
one address went from refusing most sign-ins to refusing none: as two instances behind a load
balancer, 30,000 people were carried through 804,332 requests in 25 minutes with no error. The dated
report, with the hardware, settings and raw results, is on the project site under Reviews and reports. Nothing a client sees changes — the
endpoints, tokens, discovery and configuration are as in 2.3.0 — and the README's "Running at scale"
has the settings.

* **Lookups use indexes.** Every sign-in and token request compared `lower(column)` to a value,
  which no index could serve: a sign-in read the whole user table three times and the access-mapping
  table four. They now ask for the stored value first and fall back to a `lower()` index.
* **The first start adds the missing indexes to an existing database**, including
  `refresh_tokens.session_id` and the `expires_at` columns. Never a unique index, and never fatal.
* **A confidential client's secret is verified once, then remembered** for
  `Oidc:ClientSecretCacheSeconds` (300). It was a full PBKDF2 — 40 ms of a core — on every token
  request. Only a correct secret is remembered; replacing the secret retires the entry.
* **Tenants, clients, scopes and the signing key are kept for `Oidc:ReferenceCacheSeconds`** (30).
  A change made on an instance applies there at once. Nothing is refused on a cached copy: before a
  request is turned down for what a client record says, the record is read again, so a new secret,
  redirect URI or scope works on every instance immediately. Only a change that takes something
  away reaches other instances within that time. Set 0 to read the database every time. Signing
  keys are imported once instead of once per token.
* **Password hashing is bounded** (`Oidc:MaxConcurrentPasswordHashes`, half the cores), so a
  sign-in storm no longer starves people who are already signed in. Nobody is turned away unless
  `Oidc:MaxPasswordHashWaitSeconds` is set.
* **More than one instance works without configuration.** The data-protection key ring is kept in
  the server's database on PostgreSQL and MySQL (`DataProtectionKeys: auto`); it used to
  sit in a folder per machine, so the sign-in form drawn by one instance was refused by the next.
  A host that configures its own key storage keeps it. The keys already on the machine are copied
  into the database the first time, so the upgrade signs nobody out.
* **Failed sign-ins are counted atomically.** Concurrent guesses at one account all read the same
  count, so the lockout saw a fraction of them.
* **The purge also removes refresh tokens whose session has ended**, and can trim the audit trail
  (`Oidc:AuditRetentionDays`, off by default). Revoking a session, a token family, a user or a
  client is one statement instead of loading every row.
* **The audit trail is written in batches off the request path.** Error rows are written at all:
  they were being discarded before they reached the database.
* **Requests wait for the start-up bootstrap** instead of racing ahead of it.

2.3.0 — .NET 10 and EF Core 10. Nothing else changes.

.NET 9 left support on 2026-11-10; .NET 10 is the long-term support release. This release moves the
package onto it and changes nothing a client or a user can see: the endpoints, the discovery
document, tokens, sign-in, consent, the admin console, the configuration and the database schema are
as in 2.2.1. Every client that works with a 2.2.x provider works with 2.3.0 unchanged, so the
provider and its clients can be upgraded in either order.

Before upgrading:
* **Move the host to .NET 10 first.** Target net10.0, build with the .NET 10 SDK and run on the
  ASP.NET Core 10 runtime (container image mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0; on App Service, the
  .NET 10 stack). A net9.0 host fails restore with NU1202. A host that stays on net9.0 stays on
  2.2.1, the last net9.0 release.
* **Raise the host's own pins.** A host that references EF Core, an EF provider,
  Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.* or Microsoft.IdentityModel.* directly moves them to the
  versions below, or drops them. Keep every Microsoft.IdentityModel package on one version: a split
  graph builds, then fails at the first sign-in.
* ASP.NET Core 10's own breaking changes apply to the host's code as to any app. None of them
  changes what this package serves; its management and data APIs already answered 401/403 rather
  than redirecting.

Databases: nothing to run. A database built by 2.2.x under EF Core 9 opens as it is, and the
start-up schema sync is unchanged. Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.4, against databases
created by the 2.2.1 build.

Version updates:
* Target framework: net9.0 → net10.0.
* Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore and Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite: 9.0.19 → 10.0.15.
* Npgsql.EntityFrameworkCore.PostgreSQL: 9.0.4 → 10.0.4, which needs EF Core 10.0.15 or later.
* MySql.EntityFrameworkCore: 9.0.17 → 10.0.12. It brings MySql.Data 26.10.0, which no longer pulls
  in Microsoft.IdentityModel 7.5.0.
* Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect: 9.0.10 → 10.0.15.
* Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens, Microsoft.IdentityModel.Protocols.OpenIdConnect and
  System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt: 8.8.0 → 8.23.0, still one version across the graph.

2.2.1 — 2.2.0 republished through the release workflow, which also created the GitHub release. The
published files differ from 2.2.0 only in the version number.

2.2.0 — security release. Upgrade every Ark IdP and every app using an Ark client library.

Follows a full review of the provider and the four client libraries, done because apps now use Ark
for customer-facing sign-in (site/security/2026-11-20-security-review.html in the repo). Every
high-severity finding was confirmed on a running provider, fixed, and checked again.

What you will notice:
* **Everyone signs in once more.** The single sign-on cookie is now a random secret, and the sid
  claim in tokens is its SHA-256 hash. Before this, any token was enough to rebuild the cookie and
  take over the user's session. Sessions created before the upgrade are not recognised.
* **New accounts need a real DefaultPw** (or UserPasswordMode=email_based). If it is unset or still
  a <<placeholder>>, account creation fails with 409 default_password_unset.
* **The legacy onboard/* routes** accept only the machine client's bearer token, and they never
  change an existing account. Before this, the console cookie was enough to reset any password. Use
  v1/provision/* for new integrations.

Also fixed:
* Codes, refresh tokens, device codes, PAR requests, introspection and revocation are checked
  against the tenant as well as the client. A client_id is unique only within its tenant, so a
  token could be minted at another tenant.
* A private_key_jwt client must present its assertion. Before this, the token endpoint treated it
  as public and accepted its client_id alone.
* The console grids escape registered data, which closes a stored XSS through a client name.
  Dynamic registration refuses markup in client_name and a client_id that names a user.
* A refresh re-checks the user's access mapping. In the zero-config host, every console request
  re-checks the operator's account, console mapping and admin claim, so removing an operator takes
  effect immediately.
* Both sign-in pages show one message for every credential failure. Every failure counts towards
  the lockout, whether or not the username exists.
* An id_token_hint skips the logout confirmation only when it names a session being ended, so
  another page can no longer sign a visitor out without asking.
* A tenant update no longer returns the private signing key.
* PAR payloads are capped at 16 KB. Expired grants are purged on a timer
  (ark_oauth_server:Oidc:CleanupIntervalMinutes, default 60, 0 turns it off).
* The setup wizard skips the setup code only for a loopback connection with a loopback Host.

Still open: no built-in rate limiting (rate-limit the sign-in, token, PAR, device and registration
endpoints at your edge), no password policy, and provisioned accounts share an initial password.

The npm Node client is renamed ark-oauth-client-node from this release. The API is unchanged.

2.1.6 — a landing page after sign-in. Additive.

* **The wizard asks where sign-in lands.** The Server step has a landing page, prefilled with the
  public URL (which opens the console). A page of this app is stored as a path in
  ark_oauth_server:Admin:LandingUrl, so it survives a change of public URL; an address elsewhere is
  stored as given. Sign-in's own routes are refused, since landing there would loop.
* **The page you were on wins.** The choice is made once the tokens are validated: a sign-in
  started on the way to a page (carried through the IdP in state, as before) goes back to it; one
  started at / lands on the landing page.
* **/ark-idp/signin?returnUrl=/a/page** signs in and goes there, for a host page's "Sign in" link.
  A returnUrl that is not a local path is ignored. The auth-error page's "Try again" uses it.
* Unchanged for existing servers: no LandingUrl means / ends in the console, as it did.

2.1.3 — start with nothing configured: the setup wizard. Additive.

* **Two lines, no appsettings.** builder.AddArkIdp() and app.UseArkIdp(). Started with no TenantId or
  no connection string, every browser request goes to /ark-idp/setup (other requests get 503
  setup_required), and the wizard collects the organization, logos, public URL, tenant, database
  (SQLite / PostgreSQL / MySQL, with a connection test), the RS256 signing key (generated, 2048 to
  4096 bits, or imported from PEM), the administrator, users and SMTP (with a test message),
  protocol options, CORS origins and a machine client secret.
* **The same process becomes the IdP.** Install writes ark-idp-data/settings.json, creates and seeds
  the database with what was entered, and reloads configuration. The console's sign-in options and
  the CORS policy follow the reload, so / leads straight to the sign-in page. No restart.
* **Secrets stay out of the file.** The administrator password and machine secret are stored only as
  hashes, the signing key only in signing_keys. settings.json is 0600, its directory ignores itself
  in git, and it sits below user secrets, environment and command line, so any value can still be
  overridden. Logos are stored beside it and served from /ark-idp/branding, so emails can show them.
* **Not a race to the first visitor.** From the server's own machine the wizard is open; from
  anywhere else it needs the setup code printed in the start-up log. Setup:RequireToken asks for it
  everywhere; Setup:Enabled=false removes the wizard; Setup:DataPath moves the directory (containers).
* **The keys, once, in a file.** The last screen downloads the issuer, the signing key pair (kid,
  public and private PEM) and the machine client id and secret as JSON or Excel (.xlsx), built in
  the browser; the server never returns the private key or the secret again.
* **Built-in console sign-in.** AddArkIdp registers a cookie plus the framework's OIDC handler against
  this same server, with discovery and keys read in-process rather than fetched from its own public
  address. Hosts that bring Ark.oAuth.Client keep doing so (AddArkIdp(o => o.ConsoleSignIn = false),
  or the existing calls).
* **Existing hosts are unchanged.** A server configured through appsettings or the environment never
  sees the wizard. UseArkAuthData now puts the wizard in front of the bootstrap, so hosts built on
  the lower-level calls get it too when they start unconfigured. An existing Ark database can be
  attached through the wizard instead of seeded.
* New dependency: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect 9.0.x (IdentityModel stays on
  8.8.0).

Also in 2.1.3 — themes and text size chosen by the viewer, and a "Powered by" mark.

* **Appearance picker on every page the package draws.** Sign-in, consent, device, signed-out,
  error, password reset, the admin console and the setup wizard all carry an Appearance button:
  System, Light, Dark, Midnight, Graphite, Forest, Rose, Paper, High contrast, High contrast dark,
  or Custom (light/dark mode, accent and background, with borders, muted text and button labels
  derived to stay readable). Text size from 80% to 160%, every font-size following one variable.
* **Saved per browser, applied before first paint.** localStorage on the IdP's origin, so a choice
  made at sign-in holds in the console, and other open tabs follow. Under the wizard's strict CSP
  too: values are set through CSSOM, never inline styles. Without storage, or without the script,
  the pages render exactly as before.
* **Powered by Ark Identity Server.** The Ark shield under the sign-in card, in the console footer
  and as the wizard's mark. New anonymous assets at /ark-admin/asset/: ark-theme.js, ark-theme.css,
  ark-shield-64.png, ark-shield-512.png. Optional: ark_oauth_server:ShowPoweredBy=false hides it on
  the sign-in pages and in the console footer (the version stays); the setup wizard asks.
* The password-reset confirmation page (/oauth/PwdResetThank) is rebuilt on the shared layout; it was
  the last page of the reset flow still on its own stylesheet.

2.0.14 — the management API answers to the operator only. BREAKING.

* **The package decides who may call /api/oauth/v1/….** It used to be a bare [Authorize] against the
  host's default scheme: with the console cookie as the default, any account mapped to the console
  client could create clients and reset secrets in every tenant; with a bearer scheme as the default,
  any token this server issued could. The ArkOperator policy admits the operator's console session
  (AdminUser:Username, or an admin claim on the console mapping) and bearer tokens issued to
  {TenantId}_machine with client.register — validated with this server's own keys, no host wiring.
  Everyone else gets 401/403 JSON, never a sign-in redirect. Upgrade: give other console users the
  admin claim, and delete any bearer scheme a host added for this API.
* **The machine client's secret from configuration.** ark_oauth_server:Management:MachineClientSecret
  is applied on start-up and rotated by changing it, so a pipeline-built deployment can provision on
  first boot. At least 16 characters. While set, the console refuses to regenerate that secret.
* **client.register cannot be self-granted.** Provisioning and dynamic registration refuse it; only an
  operator grants it in the console.
* **/api/migration is off by default** (Management:AllowMigrationEndpoint) and answers 404 while off.
* Optional Management:OperatorDeviceClients admits operator-approved device-code tokens, for a CLI.

Also in 2.0.14 — export, import and factory reset, on an operator-only Data page.

* **Export everything.** One JSON file with every mapped table and column — tenants, signing keys,
  clients (with secret hashes), users (with password hashes), access mappings, scopes, claims,
  sessions, refresh tokens, consents, audit trail — plus the app settings, secrets redacted unless
  asked for. Read from the EF model, so a column a later release adds is exported without a change
  here. Optionally encrypted with a passphrase (AES-256-GCM, PBKDF2-SHA256), always checksummed.
* **Import that says what it will do before it does it.** Analyse works out all three modes —
  replace, merge keeping existing records, merge taking the file's — against the database as it is,
  row by row. Rows that cannot be loaded safely (case-only collisions, broken references, duplicate
  names, unsafe redirect URIs, conflicting key material, expired grants…) are excluded by a named
  rule along with everything that depends on them; the rest loads. Apply runs the chosen plan in one
  transaction and refuses if the plan changed since it was shown.
* **Factory reset.** Empties every table and runs the same seed a new database gets — after first
  checking the seed can run, so a reset can never leave a server nobody can sign in to.
* **Additive.** No schema change, no migration, no change to an existing route. Switches under
  ark_oauth_server:Admin:DataTools (Enabled, AllowReset, AllowImport, AllowReplace,
  MaxImportMegabytes), all on by default. Specified in API-GUIDE.md.

2.0.3 and earlier — summarised in MIGRATION.md, which ships in this package. The full text is in the
release notes of 2.4.1 on nuget.org: nuget.org takes 35,000 characters at most.
title: Ark Identity Server — OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect provider
